Let me build the response. This is a long, dense technical/research synthesis request \\\\u2014 Tiger's preferences favor token-dense, no-padding output. Given the breadth (Norway EHR, cross-border flow, audit/consent/minimisation, innovation, research papers, EU parallels), this is an extended response. Prose with light headers fits Claude's formatting guidance for technical reference content.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Norway's EHR infrastructure, cross-border flow under MyHealth@EU, and the innovation pipeline\\\\n\\\\n## Part 1 \\\\u2014 How Norway runs its EHR estate\\\\n\\\\nNorway's health system is built on a **layered national infrastructure** rather than a single monolithic EHR. The shared services that everything plugs into are Helsenorge, Kjernejournal, e-resept, HelseID, Norsk Helsenett, and a shared medication-list development effort \\\\u2014 alongside Helseplattformen and DIPS as the actual hospital EHR products.\\\\n\\\\nThe pieces, briefly:\\\\n\\\\n- **Norsk Helsenett (NHN)** \\\\u2014 the closed, secure network all healthcare actors connect through. NHN is the state enterprise responsible for developing and maintaining the national ICT infrastructure for secure communication and sharing of health and personal information among healthcare professionals, including the electronic prescription system. Think of it as the trusted backbone \\\\u2014 no Helsenett certificate, no traffic.\\\\n- **Kjernejournal (Summary Care Record)** \\\\u2014 a digital record providing access to essential health information such as allergies, medications, and vaccinations. This is the national-level \\\\\\\"minimum dataset\\\\\\\" that any treating clinician in Norway can pull.\\\\n- **E-resept** \\\\u2014 the national e-prescription rail. Prescribers, pharmacies and suppliers exchange via standardised messages routed through the central prescription database (Reseptformidleren).\\\\n- **Helsenorge.no** \\\\u2014 the digital gateway for citizens to access medical records, book appointments, and consult with healthcare providers online. Citizen-facing portal, BankID-authenticated.\\\\n- **HelseID** \\\\u2014 the OIDC-based identity broker for healthcare professionals and systems. This is what carries the *who-are-you* and *what-role* claims into every transaction.\\\\n- **Helseplattformen** \\\\u2014 the regional Epic implementation in Central Norway (Helse Midt), one shared EHR across hospitals, GPs and municipalities in that region. Controversial rollout, heavy ongoing implementation research.\\\\n- **DIPS** \\\\u2014 the dominant hospital EHR vendor across the other three regions (Helse S\\\\u00f8r-\\\\u00d8st, Vest, Nord).\\\\n- **Helseanalyseplattformen / Helsedataservice** \\\\u2014 the secondary-use side; covered in Part 4.\\\\n\\\\n**Standards stack.** Norway is migrating from older message-based exchange toward **HL7 FHIR R4** as the national interchange standard. On a national level, helsenorge.no, the Welfare Technology programme and SFM (Central Prescription Module in ePrescription solution) have FHIR interfaces in production. Other examples where FHIR is used include Patient Test Results (Pasientens pr\\\\u00f8vesvar), the Health Data Programme and Helseplattformen. HL7 Norway publishes the national basisprofiler-r4 on GitHub and Simplifier \\\\u2014 these constrain the international FHIR resources for Norwegian use (NIN-based patient identifiers, HPR provider identifiers, Norwegian code systems). SNOMED CT and openEHR are also part of the architectural vocabulary, with terminology governance under Direktoratet for e-helse / Helsedirektoratet.\\\\n\\\\n**The \\\\\\\"new rules\\\\\\\" piece.** The big regulatory shift coming at Norway is **EHDS via the EEA**. As Norway is not part of the EU, the EHDS Regulation will not automatically apply to Norway. However, the EHDS Regulation has been considered EEA relevant, meaning it is likely to be implemented in Norway. The EHDS Regulation will first be implemented in Norway when there is a formal decision by the EEA Council. The Norwegian Health Directorate has also been tasked with analysing the impact of the EHDS Regulation on Norway. Helsedirektoratet has already produced an EHDS gap analysis (April 2025) mapping where Norwegian law and infrastructure diverge from the Regulation.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Part 2 \\\\u2014 What happens when a Norwegian gets treated in Spain (the actual mechanics)\\\\n\\\\nThis is the **cross-border flow** under MyHealth@EU (formerly eHDSI). Spain and Norway being a real example matters because of the long-standing Norwegian elderly-care presence on the Spanish coast.\\\\n\\\\n### The architecture in one diagram-worth of words\\\\n\\\\nEvery participating country runs exactly one **National Contact Point for eHealth (NCPeH)**. According to Article 6 of Directive 2011/24/EU, each member state must designate one or more National Contact Points for cross-border healthcare. For e-health issues, the eHealth Network has decided that there should be only one national NCPeH per country. The NCPeH is the *only* gateway that talks to other countries' NCPeHs.\\\\n\\\\nFor Norway, the Norwegian connection project to MyHealth@EU started in January 2023 with a planned duration of 36 months and production go-live for piloting set for 2025. The work is carried out in close cooperation between Helsedirektoratet and Norsk Helsenett SF. Norway aims to establish PS-B and eP-B services. It participated in PPT testing in March/April 2024 with no reported issues. For go-live piloting in 2025, two municipalities have been identified. So as of now, Norway is in **late-stage piloting**, joining the network in 2025 alongside Austria, Cyprus, Denmark, Hungary, Iceland, Italy, Romania, Sweden and Slovenia.\\\\n\\\\nThe two services in scope at launch are:\\\\n- **eP (ePrescription)** \\\\u2014 your Norwegian prescription gets dispensed at a Spanish pharmacy\\\\n- **PS (Patient Summary)** \\\\u2014 a Spanish doctor pulls your essential medical info from Norway\\\\n\\\\nFuture waves add **OrCD (Original Clinical Documents), Laboratory Results, Medical Imaging, Hospital Discharge Reports** \\\\u2014 these are the priority categories that by March 2031, for primary use, should be operational in all EU Member States: electronic imaging, medical results and discharge reports.\\\\n\\\\n### The actual pull request \\\\u2014 step by step\\\\n\\\\nScenario: You're in M\\\\u00e1laga, walk into a clinic with chest pain, the Spanish GP needs your meds list and history.\\\\n\\\\n1. **Identification.** You present a national ID document. The Spanish HCP enters identifying traits into their EHR's MyHealth@EU portal \\\\u2014 typically combinations of birth date, name, document number. The Spanish system has no idea who you are in the Norwegian system yet.\\\\n\\\\n2. **Country resolution & XCPD.** The Spanish NCPeH (Country B in eHDSI jargon \\\\u2014 the country *of treatment*) determines this is a Norwegian patient and issues a **Cross-Community Patient Discovery (IHE XCPD)** query to the Norwegian NCPeH (Country A \\\\u2014 country *of affiliation*). The query carries the patient identifiers.\\\\n\\\\n3. **Norwegian patient match.** A mechanism is triggered on the PS-A, eP-A CDA Server, which is responsible for searching the exact combination of the given patient's ID and date of birth in the SQL database cluster. If unique match, an internal Norwegian patient ID is returned. If not, the request fails with a defined error code \\\\u2014 no fuzzy matching across borders.\\\\n\\\\n4. **HCP authentication & assertions.** Before any clinical data moves, the Spanish HCP must be authenticated and authorised. The Spanish NCPeH issues two SAML 2.0 assertions: an **HCP Identity Assertion** (who is the doctor, what's their role, which organisation) and a **TRC \\\\u2014 Treatment Relationship Confirmation Assertion** (the doctor has asserted a treatment relationship with this specific patient, with timestamp). These assertions ride with every subsequent request.\\\\n\\\\n5. **Consent check on the Norwegian side.** The Norwegian NCPeH checks whether the patient has a valid cross-border sharing consent on file. This is the **policy enforcement point**. Norway's consent posture for cross-border is opt-in via Helsenorge (you actively enable cross-border sharing \\\\u2014 Norway hasn't gone the broad opt-out route some countries use). If no consent \\\\u2192 request denied, audit logged, nothing returned.\\\\n\\\\n6. **XCA Document Query/Retrieve.** The Spanish NCPeH issues an **IHE XCA (Cross-Community Access)** query, then a retrieve, against the Norwegian NCPeH. OpenNCP provides XCPD, XCA List, XCA queries and PS/eD to HTM transformation services. The Norwegian side returns a Patient Summary as an **HL7 CDA R2 Level 3 document** (structured XML, not free text) following the European Electronic Health Record Exchange Format (EEHRxF) / International Patient Summary (IPS) profile.\\\\n\\\\n7. **Pivot translation.** This is the elegant bit. The PS isn't translated Norwegian\\\\u2192Spanish directly. The Norwegian NCPeH converts the source from Norwegian local representation to a **pivot CDA in English** (using SNOMED CT, ATC for drugs, LOINC for labs, EDQM for dose forms). The Spanish NCPeH then converts pivot\\\\u2192Spanish for display. When you request the patient's ePrescription via your computer, you will receive it in the patient's language and in your language. The ePrescription is automatically translated in your own language by the underlying digital infrastructure. This is why coded data matters so much \\\\u2014 free-text \\\\\\\"kl\\\\u00f8e i halsen\\\\\\\" won't translate; SNOMED `162397003` will.\\\\n\\\\n8. **Display to clinician.** The Spanish HCP sees the PS in Spanish, with the Norwegian original available as a \\\\\\\"friendly copy.\\\\\\\" Treatment proceeds.\\\\n\\\\n9. **For ePrescription specifically:** the Spanish pharmacist queries with the patient's ID, receives the eP, dispenses, and sends back an **eDispensation** message that propagates back to Norway so the Norwegian system knows the medication was collected (and your e-resept is decremented).\\\\n\\\\n### Authorisation, consent and minimisation \\\\u2014 where each is enforced\\\\n\\\\n| Concern | Enforced at | Mechanism |\\\\n|---|---|---|\\\\n| **Authentication** of the HCP | Country B NCPeH | SAML HCP Identity Assertion, X.509 certificates, 2-way TLS between NCPeHs |\\\\n| **Authorisation** (role-based: doctor vs nurse vs pharmacist) | Country B + Country A | Role attribute in HCP assertion, validated against eHDSI role catalogue. eHDSI defines specific IHE permissions required to perform a dispense operation (XDR). |\\\\n| **Consent** | Country A (patient's home country) | Policy decision/enforcement point at Country A NCPeH. Country A is the source of truth for the patient's preferences |\\\\n| **Treatment relationship** | Country B asserts, Country A trusts (but logs) | TRC assertion in SAML |\\\\n| **Purpose-of-use** | Country B asserts | Purpose-of-use code (TREATMENT, EMERGENCY) in assertion. Break-glass / emergency override is a defined code with extra logging |\\\\n| **Data minimisation** | Country A | PS is by definition a *summary* \\\\u2014 IPS scope is bounded (allergies, current meds, problems, immunisations, recent procedures, devices). The full Norwegian EHR is not exposed. ePrescription is one specific dispensable item, not the prescription history |\\\\n| **Transport security** | Both NCPeHs | 2-way TLS, message-level XML Digital Signatures, encryption |\\\\n\\\\n### Audits \\\\u2014 at every node, in a standard format\\\\n\\\\nAudit is the spine of trust here. The standard is **IHE ATNA (Audit Trail and Node Authentication)**. ATNA is the prime security profile in the IHE toolbox. The profile is composed of three things: reasonable access controls (a functional requirement, IHE doesn't further define it), node authentication, and audit logging.\\\\n\\\\nWhat gets logged, on **both** the Norwegian and Spanish sides, for the same transaction:\\\\n\\\\n- **WHO** queried (HCP identity, organisation, role)\\\\n- **WHAT** patient was queried (de-identified reference where regulations require)\\\\n- **WHEN** with sub-second timestamp\\\\n- **WHERE** (source/destination NCPeH endpoints)\\\\n- **WHY** (purpose-of-use code)\\\\n- **OUTCOME** (success, failure, partial)\\\\n- **WHICH** document/event-codes (IHE transaction IDs)\\\\n\\\\nThe general guidance is to log the query event with the query parameters and not the result of the query. The result of a query may be very large and is likely to be of limited value vs. the overhead. So the audit captures the *fact of access*, not the clinical payload.\\\\n\\\\nThe audit standards stack: ASTM E2147 set up the concept of security audit logs for healthcare including accounting of disclosures; IETF RFC 3881 defined the information model; DICOM Audit Log Message made the information model normative and defined vocabulary, transport binding and schema; IHE ATNA defines the grouping with secure transport.\\\\n\\\\nLogs flow to an **Audit Record Repository** at each NCPeH. The Norwegian patient can request an **accounting of disclosures** \\\\u2014 show me everywhere my data went \\\\u2014 through Helsenorge once the audit log feature is exposed cross-border. Applications with audit log requirements must offer a service to retrieve HL7 FHIR AuditEvent based on the Norwegian Audit profile. The application must be an AuditEvent Repository actor, meaning it must store AuditEvent and offer a retrieval service.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Part 3 \\\\u2014 EHDS and what's changing across Europe\\\\n\\\\nThe European Health Data Space Regulation (EU) 2025/327 introduces the first EU-wide legal framework governing both primary and secondary use and exchange of electronic health data across the European Union. The EHDS Regulation came into force on 26 March 2025 and will become applicable in stages, with the general date of application falling on 26 March 2027 and further major milestones following on 26 March 2029, 26 March 2031 and 26 March 2035.\\\\n\\\\nApplication milestones:\\\\n- **March 2025** \\\\u2014 entered into force; transition begins\\\\n- **March 2027** \\\\u2014 implementing acts adopted; templates for data access applications, secure processing environment requirements, dataset descriptions and the data quality and utility label begin applying\\\\n- **March 2029** \\\\u2014 key parts of the EHDS Regulation will enter into application, including, for primary use, the exchange of the first group of priority categories of health data (Patient Summaries, ePrescriptions/eDispensations) in all EU Member States. Rules on secondary use will also start to apply for most data categories.\\\\n- **March 2031** \\\\u2014 for primary use, the exchange of the second group of priority categories (medical images, lab results, and hospital discharge reports) operational. Rules on secondary use start applying for remaining categories (e.g. genomic data).\\\\n- **March 2035** \\\\u2014 third countries can apply to join HealthData@EU\\\\n\\\\nTwo infrastructure pillars under EHDS:\\\\n- **MyHealth@EU** for **primary use** (the cross-border treatment flow described in Part 2)\\\\n- **HealthData@EU** for **secondary use** \\\\u2014 research, innovation, policy. Researchers submit data access applications to national **Health Data Access Bodies (HDABs)**; data is processed in **Secure Processing Environments (SPEs)** \\\\u2014 researchers never download row-level data, they execute code inside the secure environment and only aggregate, anonymised results leave.\\\\n\\\\nBy June 2025, each EU Member State must appoint a National Digital Health Authority to oversee EHDS implementation. By January 2026, all healthcare providers and EHR vendors must certify their systems for interoperability and security compliance. By 2027, full EHDS enforcement across the EU, with penalties for non-compliant organisations. The certification regime for EHR systems is a major industry shift \\\\u2014 vendors like DIPS, Epic-via-Helseplattformen, Cerner etc. will have to demonstrate conformance to the European interoperability and security requirements.\\\\n\\\\nThe AI Act dimension is layered on top. A recent JMIR tutorial maps this: the goal is to show how AI-specific metadata can be included in HL7 CDA and FHIR messages without disrupting standard structures, ensuring both compliance and trustworthiness in AI-assisted clinical decisions. So when an AI system is used in the clinical pathway that produces data flowing through MyHealth@EU, the AI-Act provenance metadata travels with it.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Part 4 \\\\u2014 Norway's secondary-use side: Helsedataservice and Helseanalyseplattformen\\\\n\\\\nSeparate from primary-use (treatment) is **secondary use** \\\\u2014 research, public health, innovation. Norway has been building toward this for a decade.\\\\n\\\\nNorway has a structure with many users of health data for secondary purposes and a broad range of data controllers/data administrators and decision-making authorities that make decisions about access to health data. Many of the data controllers have a long history and manage most of the minimum data categories covered by EHDS. Decision-making authority for 11 statutory health registries was in 2023 transferred to Helsedataservice (HDS), at the Norwegian Institute of Public Health. Through the Health Data Programme, Norway has established an infrastructure that gathers necessary information about health registries in one place, made available via www.helsedata.no.\\\\n\\\\nThe **registry landscape** is Norway's real superpower. National statutory registries (Norwegian Patient Registry NPR, Cancer Registry, Cause of Death Registry, Medical Birth Registry, Prescription Registry/Reseptregisteret, immunisation registry SYSVAK, etc.) cover the whole population and can be linked via the **f\\\\u00f8dselsnummer** (national ID). This is what makes studies like HUNT possible \\\\u2014 the Tr\\\\u00f8ndelag Health Study has collected population data through comprehensive decennial surveys over the last four decades and has so far collected data from 240,000 participants. The participants are identified with the unique Norwegian birth number, which enables them to be followed throughout different life stages, from survey to survey, and to endpoint measures in Norwegian national health registers without attrition bias.\\\\n\\\\n**Important note on the central platform:** It was recently decided to pause work on Helseanalyseplattformen. The big-bang central analytics platform was paused, and Norway is now focusing on simplifying registry access via Helsedataservice and helsedata.no rather than building one super-platform. EHDS will likely force a re-architecture: the EU is introducing the European Health Data Space (EHDS), a new regulatory framework that will make it easier and safer to share health data in Europe, and which sets specific requirements for secure analysis rooms (Secure Processing Environments \\\\u2013 SPE), data governance, and cross-border data sharing.\\\\n\\\\nThe **FAIR SPUHiN project** (Secure Provision and Use of Health Data in Norway) is the current work defining what a \\\\\\\"secure analysis room\\\\\\\" looks like in Norway to align with EHDS Article 73 SPE requirements.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Part 5 \\\\u2014 Innovation and research: what's happening in Norway\\\\n\\\\n### Active national initiatives\\\\n\\\\n- **BigMed** \\\\u2014 a digital platform for Precision Medicine, funded by the Norwegian Research Council and partners to address barriers to clinical implementation of precision medicine and pave the way for big data analytics. Federated learning (FL) mitigates this by training where data reside and exchanging only model updates, but practical deployments still face two core risks: (1) privacy leakage via gradients or updates (membership inference, gradient inversion) and (2) trust in the aggregator, a single point of failure that can drop, alter, or inject contributions undetected. \\\\n\\\\nWe present zkFL-Health, an architecture that combines FL with zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) and Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) to deliver privacy-preserving, verifiably correct collaborative training for medical AI. Clients locally train and commit their updates; the aggregator operates within a TEE to compute the global update and produces a succinct ZK proof (via Halo2/Nova) that it used exactly the committed inputs and the correct aggregation rule, without revealing any client update to the host. Verifier nodes validate the proof and record cryptographic commitments on-chain, providing an immutable audit trail and removing the need to trust any single party. We outline system and threat models tailored to healthcare, the zkFL-Health protocol, security/privacy guarantees, and a performance evaluation plan spanning accuracy, privacy risk, latency, and cost. \\\\n\\\\nThis framework enables multi-institutional medical AI with strong confidentiality, integrity, and auditability, key properties for clin\\\",\\n5077:        \\\"text\\\": \\\"Travellers suffering from chronic diseases are facing obstacles when travelling either within or outside their country of residence. The shared services that everything plugs into are Helsenorge, Kjernejournal, e-resept, HelseID, Norsk Helsenett, and a shared medication-list development effort \\\\u2014 alongside Helseplattformen and DIPS as the actual hospital EHR products.\\\\n\\\\nThe pieces, briefly:\\\\n\\\\n- **Norsk Helsenett (NHN)** \\\\u2014 the closed, secure network all healthcare actors connect through. NHN is the state enterprise responsible for developing and maintaining the national ICT infrastructure for secure communication and sharing of health and personal information among healthcare professionals, including the electronic prescription system. Think of it as the trusted backbone \\\\u2014 no Helsenett certificate, no traffic.\\\\n- **Kjernejournal (Summary Care Record)** \\\\u2014 a digital record providing access to essential health information such as allergies, medications, and vaccinations. This is the national-level \\\\\\\"minimum dataset\\\\\\\" that any treating clinician in Norway can pull.\\\\n- **E-resept** \\\\u2014 the national e-prescription rail. Prescribers, pharmacies and suppliers exchange via standardised messages routed through the central prescription database (Reseptformidleren).\\\\n- **Helsenorge.no** \\\\u2014 the digital gateway for citizens to access medical records, book appointments, and consult with healthcare providers online. Citizen-facing portal, BankID-authenticated.\\\\n- **HelseID** \\\\u2014 the OIDC-based identity broker for healthcare professionals and systems. This is what carries the *who-are-you* and *what-role* claims into every transaction.\\\\n- **Helseplattformen** \\\\u2014 the regional Epic implementation in Central Norway (Helse Midt), one shared EHR across hospitals, GPs and municipalities in that region. Controversial rollout, heavy ongoing implementation research.\\\\n- **DIPS** \\\\u2014 the dominant hospital EHR vendor across the other three regions (Helse S\\\\u00f8r-\\\\u00d8st, Vest, Nord).\\\\n- **Helseanalyseplattformen / Helsedataservice** \\\\u2014 the secondary-use side; covered in Part 4.\\\\n\\\\n**Standards stack.** Norway is migrating from older message-based exchange toward **HL7 FHIR R4** as the national interchange standard. On a national level, helsenorge.no, the Welfare Technology programme and SFM (Central Prescription Module in ePrescription solution) have FHIR interfaces in production. Other examples where FHIR is used include Patient Test Results (Pasientens pr\\\\u00f8vesvar), the Health Data Programme and Helseplattformen. HL7 Norway publishes the national basisprofiler-r4 on GitHub and Simplifier \\\\u2014 these constrain the international FHIR resources for Norwegian use (NIN-based patient identifiers, HPR provider identifiers, Norwegian code systems). SNOMED CT and openEHR are also part of the architectural vocabulary, with terminology governance under Direktoratet for e-helse / Helsedirektoratet.\\\\n\\\\n**The \\\\\\\"new rules\\\\\\\" piece.** The big regulatory shift coming at Norway is **EHDS via the EEA**. As Norway is not part of the EU, the EHDS Regulation will not automatically apply to Norway. However, the EHDS Regulation has been considered EEA relevant, meaning it is likely to be implemented in Norway. The EHDS Regulation will first be implemented in Norway when there is a formal decision by the EEA Council. The Norwegian Health Directorate has also been tasked with analysing the impact of the EHDS Regulation on Norway. Helsedirektoratet has already produced an EHDS gap analysis (April 2025) mapping where Norwegian law and infrastructure diverge from the Regulation.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Part 2 \\\\u2014 What happens when a Norwegian gets treated in Spain (the actual mechanics)\\\\n\\\\nThis is the **cross-border flow** under MyHealth@EU (formerly eHDSI). Spain and Norway being a real example matters because of the long-standing Norwegian elderly-care presence on the Spanish coast.\\\\n\\\\n### The architecture in one diagram-worth of words\\\\n\\\\nEvery participating country runs exactly one **National Contact Point for eHealth (NCPeH)**. According to Article 6 of Directive 2011/24/EU, each member state must designate one or more National Contact Points for cross-border healthcare. For e-health issues, the eHealth Network has decided that there should be only one national NCPeH per country. The NCPeH is the *only* gateway that talks to other countries' NCPeHs.\\\\n\\\\nFor Norway, the Norwegian connection project to MyHealth@EU started in January 2023 with a planned duration of 36 months and production go-live for piloting set for 2025. The work is carried out in close cooperation between Helsedirektoratet and Norsk Helsenett SF. Norway aims to establish PS-B and eP-B services. It participated in PPT testing in March/April 2024 with no reported issues. For go-live piloting in 2025, two municipalities have been identified. So as of now, Norway is in **late-stage piloting**, joining the network in 2025 alongside Austria, Cyprus, Denmark, Hungary, Iceland, Italy, Romania, Sweden and Slovenia.\\\\n\\\\nThe two services in scope at launch are:\\\\n- **eP (ePrescription)** \\\\u2014 your Norwegian prescription gets dispensed at a Spanish pharmacy\\\\n- **PS (Patient Summary)** \\\\u2014 a Spanish doctor pulls your essential medical info from Norway\\\\n\\\\nFuture waves add **OrCD (Original Clinical Documents), Laboratory Results, Medical Imaging, Hospital Discharge Reports** \\\\u2014 these are the priority categories that by March 2031, for primary use, should be operational in all EU Member States: electronic imaging, medical results and discharge reports.\\\\n\\\\n### The actual pull request \\\\u2014 step by step\\\\n\\\\nScenario: You're in M\\\\u00e1laga, walk into a clinic with chest pain, the Spanish GP needs your meds list and history.\\\\n\\\\n1. **Identification.** You present a national ID document. The Spanish HCP enters identifying traits into their EHR's MyHealth@EU portal \\\\u2014 typically combinations of birth date, name, document number. The Spanish system has no idea who you are in the Norwegian system yet.\\\\n\\\\n2. **Country resolution & XCPD.** The Spanish NCPeH (Country B in eHDSI jargon \\\\u2014 the country *of treatment*) determines this is a Norwegian patient and issues a **Cross-Community Patient Discovery (IHE XCPD)** query to the Norwegian NCPeH (Country A \\\\u2014 country *of affiliation*). The query carries the patient identifiers.\\\\n\\\\n3. **Norwegian patient match.** A mechanism is triggered on the PS-A, eP-A CDA Server, which is responsible for searching the exact combination of the given patient's ID and date of birth in the SQL database cluster. If unique match, an internal Norwegian patient ID is returned. If not, the request fails with a defined error code \\\\u2014 no fuzzy matching across borders.\\\\n\\\\n4. **HCP authentication & assertions.** Before any clinical data moves, the Spanish HCP must be authenticated and authorised. The Spanish NCPeH issues two SAML 2.0 assertions: an **HCP Identity Assertion** (who is the doctor, what's their role, which organisation) and a **TRC \\\\u2014 Treatment Relationship Confirmation Assertion** (the doctor has asserted a treatment relationship with this specific patient, with timestamp). These assertions ride with every subsequent request.\\\\n\\\\n5. **Consent check on the Norwegian side.** The Norwegian NCPeH checks whether the patient has a valid cross-border sharing consent on file. This is the **policy enforcement point**. Norway's consent posture for cross-border is opt-in via Helsenorge (you actively enable cross-border sharing \\\\u2014 Norway hasn't gone the broad opt-out route some countries use). If no consent \\\\u2192 request denied, audit logged, nothing returned.\\\\n\\\\n6. **XCA Document Query/Retrieve.** The Spanish NCPeH issues an **IHE XCA (Cross-Community Access)** query, then a retrieve, against the Norwegian NCPeH. OpenNCP provides XCPD, XCA List, XCA queries and PS/eD to HTM transformation services. The Norwegian side returns a Patient Summary as an **HL7 CDA R2 Level 3 document** (structured XML, not free text) following the European Electronic Health Record Exchange Format (EEHRxF) / International Patient Summary (IPS) profile.\\\\n\\\\n7. **Pivot translation.** This is the elegant bit. The PS isn't translated Norwegian\\\\u2192Spanish directly. The Norwegian NCPeH converts the source from Norwegian local representation to a **pivot CDA in English** (using SNOMED CT, ATC for drugs, LOINC for labs, EDQM for dose forms). The Spanish NCPeH then converts pivot\\\\u2192Spanish for display. When you request the patient's ePrescription via your computer, you will receive it in the patient's language and in your language. The ePrescription is automatically translated in your own language by the underlying digital infrastructure. This is why coded data matters so much \\\\u2014 free-text \\\\\\\"kl\\\\u00f8e i halsen\\\\\\\" won't translate; SNOMED `162397003` will.\\\\n\\\\n8. **Display to clinician.** The Spanish HCP sees the PS in Spanish, with the Norwegian original available as a \\\\\\\"friendly copy.\\\\\\\" Treatment proceeds.\\\\n\\\\n9. **For ePrescription specifically:** the Spanish pharmacist queries with the patient's ID, receives the eP, dispenses, and sends back an **eDispensation** message that propagates back to Norway so the Norwegian system knows the medication was collected (and your e-resept is decremented).\\\\n\\\\n### Authorisation, consent and minimisation \\\\u2014 where each is enforced\\\\n\\\\n| Concern | Enforced at | Mechanism |\\\\n|---|---|---|\\\\n| **Authentication** of the HCP | Country B NCPeH | SAML HCP Identity Assertion, X.509 certificates, 2-way TLS between NCPeHs |\\\\n| **Authorisation** (role-based: doctor vs nurse vs pharmacist) | Country B + Country A | Role attribute in HCP assertion, validated against eHDSI role catalogue. eHDSI defines specific IHE permissions required to perform a dispense operation (XDR). |\\\\n| **Consent** | Country A (patient's home country) | Policy decision/enforcement point at Country A NCPeH. Country A is the source of truth for the patient's preferences |\\\\n| **Treatment relationship** | Country B asserts, Country A trusts (but logs) | TRC assertion in SAML |\\\\n| **Purpose-of-use** | Country B asserts | Purpose-of-use code (TREATMENT, EMERGENCY) in assertion. Break-glass / emergency override is a defined code with extra logging |\\\\n| **Data minimisation** | Country A | PS is by definition a *summary* \\\\u2014 IPS scope is bounded (allergies, current meds, problems, immunisations, recent procedures, devices). The full Norwegian EHR is not exposed. ePrescription is one specific dispensable item, not the prescription history |\\\\n| **Transport security** | Both NCPeHs | 2-way TLS, message-level XML Digital Signatures, encryption |\\\\n\\\\n### Audits \\\\u2014 at every node, in a standard format\\\\n\\\\nAudit is the spine of trust here. The standard is **IHE ATNA (Audit Trail and Node Authentication)**. ATNA is the prime security profile in the IHE toolbox. The profile is composed of three things: reasonable access controls (a functional requirement, IHE doesn't further define it), node authentication, and audit logging.\\\\n\\\\nWhat gets logged, on **both** the Norwegian and Spanish sides, for the same transaction:\\\\n\\\\n- **WHO** queried (HCP identity, organisation, role)\\\\n- **WHAT** patient was queried (de-identified reference where regulations require)\\\\n- **WHEN** with sub-second timestamp\\\\n- **WHERE** (source/destination NCPeH endpoints)\\\\n- **WHY** (purpose-of-use code)\\\\n- **OUTCOME** (success, failure, partial)\\\\n- **WHICH** document/event-codes (IHE transaction IDs)\\\\n\\\\nThe general guidance is to log the query event with the query parameters and not the result of the query. The result of a query may be very large and is likely to be of limited value vs. the overhead. So the audit captures the *fact of access*, not the clinical payload.\\\\n\\\\nThe audit standards stack: ASTM E2147 set up the concept of security audit logs for healthcare including accounting of disclosures; IETF RFC 3881 defined the information model; DICOM Audit Log Message made the information model normative and defined vocabulary, transport binding and schema; IHE ATNA defines the grouping with secure transport.\\\\n\\\\nLogs flow to an **Audit Record Repository** at each NCPeH. The Norwegian patient can request an **accounting of disclosures** \\\\u2014 show me everywhere my data went \\\\u2014 through Helsenorge once the audit log feature is exposed cross-border. Applications with audit log requirements must offer a service to retrieve HL7 FHIR AuditEvent based on the Norwegian Audit profile. The application must be an AuditEvent Repository actor, meaning it must store AuditEvent and offer a retrieval service.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Part 3 \\\\u2014 EHDS and what's changing across Europe\\\\n\\\\nThe European Health Data Space Regulation (EU) 2025/327 introduces the first EU-wide legal framework governing both primary and secondary use and exchange of electronic health data across the European Union. The EHDS Regulation came into force on 26 March 2025 and will become applicable in stages, with the general date of application falling on 26 March 2027 and further major milestones following on 26 March 2029, 26 March 2031 and 26 March 2035.\\\\n\\\\nApplication milestones:\\\\n- **March 2025** \\\\u2014 entered into force; transition begins\\\\n- **March 2027** \\\\u2014 implementing acts adopted; templates for data access applications, secure processing environment requirements, dataset descriptions and the data quality and utility label begin applying\\\\n- **March 2029** \\\\u2014 key parts of the EHDS Regulation will enter into application, including, for primary use, the exchange of the first group of priority categories of health data (Patient Summaries, ePrescriptions/eDispensations) in all EU Member States. Rules on secondary use will also start to apply for most data categories.\\\\n- **March 2031** \\\\u2014 for primary use, the exchange of the second group of priority categories (medical images, lab results, and hospital discharge reports) operational. Rules on secondary use start applying for remaining categories (e.g. genomic data).\\\\n- **March 2035** \\\\u2014 third countries can apply to join HealthData@EU\\\\n\\\\nTwo infrastructure pillars under EHDS:\\\\n- **MyHealth@EU** for **primary use** (the cross-border treatment flow described in Part 2)\\\\n- **HealthData@EU** for **secondary use** \\\\u2014 research, innovation, policy. Researchers submit data access applications to national **Health Data Access Bodies (HDABs)**; data is processed in **Secure Processing Environments (SPEs)** \\\\u2014 researchers never download row-level data, they execute code inside the secure environment and only aggregate, anonymised results leave.\\\\n\\\\nBy June 2025, each EU Member State must appoint a National Digital Health Authority to oversee EHDS implementation. By January 2026, all healthcare providers and EHR vendors must certify their systems for interoperability and security compliance. By 2027, full EHDS enforcement across the EU, with penalties for non-compliant organisations. The certification regime for EHR systems is a major industry shift \\\\u2014 vendors like DIPS, Epic-via-Helseplattformen, Cerner etc. will have to demonstrate conformance to the European interoperability and security requirements.\\\\n\\\\nThe AI Act dimension is layered on top. A recent JMIR tutorial maps this: the goal is to show how AI-specific metadata can be included in HL7 CDA and FHIR messages without disrupting standard structures, ensuring both compliance and trustworthiness in AI-assisted clinical decisions. So when an AI system is used in the clinical pathway that produces data flowing through MyHealth@EU, the AI-Act provenance metadata travels with it.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Part 4 \\\\u2014 Norway's secondary-use side: Helsedataservice and Helseanalyseplattformen\\\\n\\\\nSeparate from primary-use (treatment) is **secondary use** \\\\u2014 research, public health, innovation. Norway has been building toward this for a decade.\\\\n\\\\nNorway has a structure with many users of health data for secondary purposes and a broad range of data controllers/data administrators and decision-making authorities that make decisions about access to health data. Many of the data controllers have a long history and manage most of the minimum data categories covered by EHDS. Decision-making authority for 11 statutory health registries was in 2023 transferred to Helsedataservice (HDS), at the Norwegian Institute of Public Health. Through the Health Data Programme, Norway has established an infrastructure that gathers necessary information about health registries in one place, made available via www.helsedata.no.\\\\n\\\\nThe **registry landscape** is Norway's real superpower. National statutory registries (Norwegian Patient Registry NPR, Cancer Registry, Cause of Death Registry, Medical Birth Registry, Prescription Registry/Reseptregisteret, immunisation registry SYSVAK, etc.) cover the whole population and can be linked via the **f\\\\u00f8dselsnummer** (national ID). This is what makes studies like HUNT possible \\\\u2014 the Tr\\\\u00f8ndelag Health Study has collected population data through comprehensive decennial surveys over the last four decades and has so far collected data from 240,000 participants. The participants are identified with the unique Norwegian birth number, which enables them to be followed throughout different life stages, from survey to survey, and to endpoint measures in Norwegian national health registers without attrition bias.\\\\n\\\\n**Important note on the central platform:** It was recently decided to pause work on Helseanalyseplattformen. The big-bang central analytics platform was paused, and Norway is now focusing on simplifying registry access via Helsedataservice and helsedata.no rather than building one super-platform. EHDS will likely force a re-architecture: the EU is introducing the European Health Data Space (EHDS), a new regulatory framework that will make it easier and safer to share health data in Europe, and which sets specific requirements for secure analysis rooms (Secure Processing Environments \\\\u2013 SPE), data governance, and cross-border data sharing.\\\\n\\\\nThe **FAIR SPUHiN project** (Secure Provision and Use of Health Data in Norway) is the current work defining what a \\\\\\\"secure analysis room\\\\\\\" looks like in Norway to align with EHDS Article 73 SPE requirements.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Part 5 \\\\u2014 Innovation and research: what's happening in Norway\\\\n\\\\n### Active national initiatives\\\\n\\\\n- **BigMed** \\\\u2014 a digital platform for Precision Medicine, funded by the Norwegian Research Council and partners to address barriers to clinical implementation of precision medicine and pave the way for big data analytics. In recent years, the distributed healthcare blockchain system has been researched for solving the information isolated island problem in centralized healthcare service systems. However, there still exists a series of important problems such as the patients\\\\u2019 sensitive information security, cross-institutional data sharing, medical quality, and efficiency. In this paper, we establish a lightweight privacy-preserving mechanism for a healthcare blockchain system. First, we apply an interleaving encoder to encrypt the original EMRs. This can hide the sensitive information of EMRs to protect the patient\\\\u2019s privacy security. Second, a (t,n)-threshold lightweight message sharing scheme is presented. The EMRs are mapped to *n* different short shares, and it can be reconstructed by at least *t* shares. \\\\n\\\\nThe EMR shares rather than the original EMRs are stored in the blockchain nodes. This can guarantee high security for EMR sharing and improve the data reconstruction efficiency. Third, the indexes of the stored EMR shares are employed to generate blocks that are chained together and finally form a blockchain. The authorized data users or institutions can recover an EMR by requesting at least *t* shares of the EMR from the blockchain nodes. In this way, the healthcare blockchain system can not only facilitate the cross-institution sharing process, but also provide proper protections for the EMRs. The security proof and analysis indicate that the proposed scheme can protect the privacy and security of patients\\\\u2019 medical information.         "text": "# **Bounded Satisfiability Checking of Metric First-Order Temporal Logic**\n\nNick Feng fengnick@cs.toronto.edu University of Toronto Toronto, Ontario, Canada\n\nMehrdad Sabetzadeh mehrdad@cs.uottawa.ca University of Ottawa Ottawa, Ontario, Canada\n\n# Lina Marsso lina.marsso@utoronto.ca University of Toronto Toronto, Ontario, Canada\n\nMarsha Chechik chechik@cs.toronto.edu University of Toronto Toronto, Ontario, Canada\n\n### **ABSTRACT**\n\nLegal properties involve reasoning about data values and time. Metric first-order temporal logic (MFOTL) provides a rich formalism for specifying legal properties. While MFOTL has been successfully used for verifying legal properties over operational systems via runtime monitoring, no solution exists for MFOTL-based verification in early-stage system development captured by requirements. Given a legal property and system requirements both formalized in MFOTL, the compliance of the property can be verified on the requirements via satisfiability checking. \n\nIn this paper, we propose a practical, sound, and complete (within a given bound) satisfiability checking approach for MFOTL. The approach, based on satisfiability modulo theories (SMT), employs a counterexample-guided strategy to incrementally search for a satisfying solution. We implemented our approach using the Z3 SMT solver and evaluated it on five case studies spanning the healthcare, business administration, banking and aviation domains. Our results indicate that our approach can efficiently determine whether legal properties of interest are met, or generate counterexamples that lead to compliance violations.\n\n#### **KEYWORDS**\n\nRequirements Engineering, Metric First-order Temporal Logic (MFOTL), Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT).\n\n#### 1 INTRODUCTION\n\nSoftware systems, such as medical systems or banking systems, are increasingly required to comply with laws, regulations and policies aimed at ensuring safety, security, data protection and privacy [22, 38]. \n\nThe formalization ca",

        "text": "[formal verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_verification), where it is used to state requirements of hardware or software systems. For instance, one may wish to say that whenever a request is made, access to a resource is eventually granted, but it is never granted to two requestors simultaneously. Such a statement can conveniently be expressed in a temporal logic.\nConsider the statement \"I am hungry\". Though its meaning is constant in time, the statement's truth value can vary in time. Sometimes it is true, and sometimes false, but never simultaneously true and false. In a temporal logic, a statement can have a truth value that varies in time\u2014in contrast with an atemporal logic, which applies only to statements whose truth values are constant in time. The Regulation aims to enhance the exchange of healthcare data across Europe by strengthening individual control of health data, developing and improving a single market for digital health services and products, and establishing an efficient framework for\u2026 \u00b7 Purpose: The EHDS establishes clear rules on the secure exchange, use and reuse of health data to improve healthcare, research, innovation and policymaking. To align with the Regulation, the Norwegian health legislation will require amendments, such as in the Patient Records Act (Pasientjournalloven).
